Jordan Lifts Short-Lived Export Ban on Oil & Gas Producers, Industry Operations Resume

Jordan’s Oil & Gas Producers industry has welcomed the government’s decision to lift a temporary export ban on crude oil and refined petroleum products, resolving weeks of uncertainty and disruption in the sector. The Ministry of Industry, Trade and Supply confirmed on Monday that the ban, which had been in place since early May, was officially rescinded following discussions with industry representatives and a review of domestic supply conditions.

The measure, first announced on May 2, restricted the export of both crude oil and key refined products such as gasoline and diesel. The government cited the need to ensure adequate domestic supply amid concerns over regional instability and fluctuating international prices. According to the ministry, the ban was intended as a precaution to “safeguard the energy needs of the Jordanian market” during a period of increased demand and supply chain volatility.

The move affected several local producers, including Al-Mashreq Petrochemicals and East Jordan Oilfields, whose export shipments to neighboring markets were halted. “We had to suspend two major contracts with buyers in Lebanon and Iraq,” said Fawzi Khalil, operations director at East Jordan Oilfields. “This meant stockpiles quickly built up at our storage facilities, and some of our transport partners faced temporary layoffs.”

Industry figures indicate that the ban impacted an estimated 225,000 barrels of product, representing nearly 40% of the sector’s monthly export volume. The Jordanian Oil Producers Association (JOPA) voiced concerns early on that the restriction would strain cash flows and could risk long-term relationships with regional buyers if prolonged. “We understand the government’s rationale, but we urged for a swift review to avoid reputational damage with our trading partners,” said JOPA chairwoman Lina Haddad.

After consultations and an assessment of national reserves, the ministry determined that domestic supply had stabilized, allowing for the restriction to be lifted. In a statement, Minister of Industry, Trade and Supply Dr. Yusuf Al-Rawashdeh emphasized that the government remains committed to both energy security and the vitality of the export sector. “We have worked closely with industry stakeholders to ensure a balanced approach,” he said. “Operations may resume immediately, and we will continue to monitor market conditions.”

Industry sources report that export shipments began moving again from the Port of Aqaba on Sunday night, with companies prioritizing delayed contracts and resuming regular schedules. Analysts expect the sector to recover quickly. “The swift resolution helps restore confidence among producers and buyers,” said Sami Fadhel, an Amman-based energy analyst. “Jordan’s Oil & Gas Producers are well-positioned to regain lost ground in the coming weeks.”
